records.subagent_summary: All eight rollouts (execution 148.358, 1/8 correct) hit the same wall: they enumerate factor pairs, then globally decide the shown number is the product, which lets each speaker divide and know the partner at once, so both branches 'contradict' and the run hand-waves to a guess; two also burned the token cap looping. None ever tabulates, for one speaker, the several partner values that speaker's own view still permits, which is what the incumbent's abstract 'group candidates by the value that speaker privately knows' and 'groups whose relevant coordinate is already unique' ask for but no rollout executes. This edit swaps that jargon for the concrete count they already half-perform, at the same length and with the same ordered-elimination skeleton, so it should transfer to any announcement puzzle.

Fresh rollouts (148.359) scored 7/8; the single miss was not a strategy failure but a length overrun: that trace reached the correct x,y quadratic and then spent thousands of tokens looping on whether unequal-looking x^2/y^2 coefficients meant ellipse or circle, and never emitted a boxed answer. Rounds 4, 15 and 17 already tried adding a normalize/certify-the-circle clause to fix exactly that loop and all three lost held-out badly, so I am not re-testing that idea. Instead this is a strictly orthographic compression: the only byte changed is the diaeresis in Moebius, which costs 4 Qwen tokens as 'Mobius' costs 2. Every content word, step and ordering is byte-identical, so held-out should tie and win the shorter-hint tiebreak at 69 vs 70 tokens. No rollout ever reproduced the diacritic itself.

Rollouts scored 4/8: three failures burned the entire 16384-token budget and never closed the reasoning block (20-43 'Alternatively', 47-82 'Wait' each) even though one of them had already stated the correct exact value and then kept searching; the fourth closed but boxed a total from an overlap it asserted in prose rather than computed. Across all eight traces the incumbent's free-rotation/symmetry clause drew 0-2 symmetry or invariance words and 'extent' zero, so both are inert transfer tax, while coordinates and the sum-minus-overlap formula were used constantly and are left byte-identical. I replaced only the inert symmetry clause with the construction-plus-one-line-bound stop condition (the wording that produced this hint's second-best held-out) and deleted the inert 'extent' phrase, giving an observable reason to stop searching on any extremum problem at 160 tokens versus the incumbent's 169.

Fresh rollouts (148.361) scored 6/8. Both failures silently assume each polynomial handles exactly ONE input: one then treats the whole stretch as roots of a single difference and reports the degree alone, the other assigns one term per polynomial and reports the menu size alone. Every correct rollout instead reasons about a polynomial covering a stretch of inputs. The incumbent's counting step asks how many inputs satisfy P(x)=A+Bx but never says a polynomial may be reused for several, so the one-input reading survives and the 'never one factor alone' reminder gets quoted without effect. This edit adds that one positive licensing clause where it is needed, keeps every step the correct rollouts lean on byte-identical, and is shorter than the incumbent (668 vs 697 characters).

Six of eight rollouts were correct. Both failures solved for the unknown input value correctly, then filled in the matching output by copying/mirroring a given point's value instead of evaluating the defining relation at that input; the resulting figure was degenerate, and one rollout then spent its whole token budget doubting the setup without ever committing. This edit sharpens the incumbent's existing clause in place so the defining equation is named as the thing to evaluate at the solved value, not merely a condition to satisfy. It is one positive instruction, adds no prohibition or checklist, costs zero extra tokens (70, same as the incumbent), and leaves every clause the six successful rollouts rely on untouched, so it should transfer to any problem recovering unknown points from a curve or rule.

All 8 rollouts failed (0/8) and 6 of them explicitly asserted that a destination stack's bottom is the LAST item placed there, then priced that inverted event; the incumbent already states the correct fact abstractly but the student never applies it, so it reads the sentence and still flips the direction. The edit replaces the passive restatement with one executable action - rewrite the destination stack after every landing and see the new item sit on top - which makes arrived-first-is-bottom something the student derives rather than recalls, and drops the sum-to-one branch check that zero of 32 rollouts across four rounds ever performed, leaving the hint shorter than the incumbent.

All 8 rollouts ran to the 16k cap with no boxed answer. Six did try the shrink, but never wrote the reduced instance down: they spent most of the budget in prose re-questioning how the small case should be indexed, and three drifted into an abstract closed-form guess and then argued with themselves about it. Meanwhile the incumbent's ratio-of-consecutive-entries clause needs three solved sizes and no rollout reached even two, so it never fired. This edit spends those tokens instead on the concrete first move the rollouts lack: write the shrunken instance out as numbered equations, then solve it. Committing the small system to paper is what stops the re-derivation loop, and it transfers to any problem with an oversized parameter.

Seven of eight rollouts were correct; the loss, and both round-17 losses, failed the same way: the student correctly reduced whole-per-item to divisibility and got the gcd, then the incumbent's candidate-list framing ('the candidates are the divisors of their gcd') manufactured several options with no way to resolve them, and it spiralled and picked one arbitrarily. This replaces that enumerate-then-guess framing with a single deterministic computation - divide each total by the gcd to read off the per-item amounts - so the integrality step terminates in one value instead of a menu. Unlike rounds 2, 6 and 17 this adds no selection or tiebreak rule on top of a candidate list; it removes the list, and is two tokens shorter than the incumbent.

Three of eight rollouts solved it; the five failures all accepted the reflection ansatz and derived s correctly, then broke at the evaluation step. The incumbent's 'pairing arguments that sum to s' was read as pairing an argument with itself, so one rollout wrote p(a) = s - p(a) for an argument that was not the midpoint, got a wrong value, noticed the contradiction and boxed the bad pair anyway; the other four never formed a usable pair and burned the cap re-deriving coefficient systems. This edit states the pairing rule operationally - the partner of a is s - a, so trade an unknown argument for a known one, and only s/2 is self-paired - which should transfer to any problem where a reflection identity must be evaluated at specific inputs. Same length as the incumbent.

4/8 correct. All four failures hit the completion cap with no boxed answer, and every one died the same way: they never fixed a single reading of what one pass of the process is, re-litigating the wording verbally for thousands of tokens and producing two conflicting values for the same smallest size before running out of room. The four successes instead pinned the reading immediately by applying one pass step by step to a small labeled case, then moved up in size. The incumbent's opening 'Settle what one pass does, first' names the goal but no executable move, so the student tries to settle it by argument, which never terminates. This edit supplies the concrete move (settle it by running one pass on the smallest labeled case, then hold that reading) and should transfer to any multi-step-process question whose statement admits more than one parse. It is one token shorter than the incumbent.
